uses: Used to ease pain, swelling, and stiffness in conditions such as arthritis, back pain, dental pain, and other muscle or joint problems.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset, indigestion, nausea, or heartburn. Seek help urgently if you notice black stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Best taken with or just after food to reduce stomach irritation.
precautions: Long-term use can affect the stomach, kidneys, and heart; avoid alcohol and tell your doctor if you have ulcers, kidney disease, or are pregnant. Avoid combining with other NSAIDs.

uses: Used to treat infections caused by herpes viruses, such as cold sores, genital herpes, shingles, and chickenpox.
sideEffects: May cause nausea, headache, or diarrhea. Rarely, kidney problems can occur, so seek help if you notice much less urine or unusual tiredness.
food: Can be taken with or without food; take with plenty of water.
precautions: Works best when started early in an outbreak; drink plenty of fluids to protect the kidneys. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or are pregnant.

uses: A skin gel or cream used to treat acne by unclogging pores and reducing pimples and blackheads.
sideEffects: Commonly causes dryness, redness, peeling, stinging, or mild burning of the skin, especially in the first few weeks. This usually settles as skin adjusts.
food: Not applicable — it is applied to the skin, not swallowed.
precautions: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin and avoid eyes, lips, and broken skin. It increases sun sensitivity, so use sunscreen; results take several weeks and it should be avoided in pregnancy unless advised.

uses: Used for the short-term relief of anxiety and panic disorders.
sideEffects: Commonly causes drowsiness, dizziness, and reduced alertness. It can be habit-forming and may impair memory or coordination.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not drink alcohol or drive until you know how it affects you, and never stop it suddenly after regular use — the dose should be lowered gradually under medical guidance. It carries a risk of dependence and dangerous sedation if combined with opioids or other sedatives.

uses: Used to relieve heartburn, acid indigestion, an upset stomach, and bloating or gas.
sideEffects: May cause constipation (from the aluminium) or loose stools (from the magnesium); the two ingredients tend to balance each other. Simethicone helps break up gas bubbles.
food: Usually taken after meals and at bedtime, or when symptoms occur; follow the label.
precautions: Antacids can reduce absorption of other medicines, so separate them by a couple of hours. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or need it frequently over a long period.

uses: Used to loosen and thin mucus in the airways, making coughs with phlegm easier to clear in chest infections and bronchitis.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; may occasionally cause mild stomach upset, nausea, or a dry mouth or throat.
food: Usually taken after meals with water.
precautions: Stop and seek medical advice if you develop a skin rash, as rare serious skin reactions have been reported. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or have stomach ulcers.

uses: Used to lower high blood pressure and to prevent chest pain (angina) by relaxing and widening blood vessels.
sideEffects: May cause ankle or leg swelling, flushing, headache, or dizziness, especially when first starting. These often ease with time.
food: Can be taken with or without food, ideally at the same time each day.
precautions: Do not stop it suddenly without advice, as this can worsen blood pressure or chest pain. Rise slowly from sitting or lying to avoid dizziness; grapefruit may increase its effect.

uses: Used to treat a range of bacterial infections, such as chest, ear, throat, sinus, dental, and urinary infections.
sideEffects: May cause diarrhea, nausea, or a skin rash. Seek urgent help for signs of a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, or a spreading rash.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not take if you are allergic to penicillin. Finish the full course even if you feel better, and tell your doctor about any previous antibiotic reactions.

uses: A combination antibiotic used for bacterial infections that may resist amoxicillin alone, such as certain chest, sinus, ear, dental, urinary, and skin infections.
sideEffects: Diarrhea and nausea are common and can be more frequent than with amoxicillin alone. Seek urgent help for signs of a serious allergic reaction or, rarely, yellowing of the skin or eyes.
food: Best taken with food or at the start of a meal to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Do not take if you are allergic to penicillin. Complete the full course, and tell your doctor if you have had liver problems with this medicine before.

uses: Medicated lozenges used to relieve sore throat and minor mouth or throat infections by helping to reduce germs locally.
sideEffects: Generally very well tolerated; may occasionally cause mild mouth or tongue irritation.
food: Can be used as needed; let each lozenge dissolve slowly in the mouth rather than chewing.
precautions: For short-term relief only — see a doctor if a sore throat is severe, comes with high fever, or lasts more than a few days. Check the label for sugar content if you have diabetes.

uses: Used to prevent and treat blood clots, including in conditions such as atrial fibrillation and deep vein clots, lowering the risk of stroke.
sideEffects: The main risk is bleeding — watch for unusual bruising, nosebleeds, blood in urine or stool, or bleeding that won't stop. Seek urgent help for any heavy or uncontrolled bleeding.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Never stop it on your own, as this raises stroke or clot risk. Tell all your doctors and dentists you take it before any procedure, and avoid combining with other blood thinners or NSAIDs unless advised.

uses: Used in low doses to help prevent heart attacks and strokes by keeping blood from clotting, and in higher doses for pain, fever, and inflammation.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset, heartburn, or increased bleeding and bruising. Seek help for black stools, vomiting blood, or ringing in the ears.
food: Take with or after food to reduce stomach irritation.
precautions: Should not be given to children or teenagers with viral illness due to the risk of Reye's syndrome. Tell your doctor if you have ulcers or take other blood thinners, and do not stop heart-protective aspirin without advice.

uses: Used to lower 'bad' cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, often alongside a healthy diet.
sideEffects: May cause muscle aches, headache, or mild digestive upset. Report unexplained, severe, or persistent muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness to your doctor promptly.
food: Can be taken with or without food, at the same time each day; often taken in the evening.
precautions: Avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice, which can raise drug levels. Tell your doctor about liver problems, heavy alcohol use, or if you become pregnant.

uses: Used to relieve allergy symptoms such as a runny or itchy nose, sneezing, and itchy or watery eyes.
sideEffects: May cause a bitter taste, mild nasal irritation, or slight drowsiness. Eye drops can cause brief stinging.
food: Not applicable — it is used in the nose or eyes, not swallowed.
precautions: Avoid getting nasal spray in the eyes; be cautious with alcohol or other sedatives as drowsiness can occur. Follow the label for how often to use it.

uses: A nasal spray combining an antihistamine and a steroid to relieve moderate to severe allergy symptoms such as congestion, runny nose, sneezing, and itching.
sideEffects: May cause a bitter taste, nosebleeds, nasal dryness or irritation, or headache.
food: Not applicable — it is sprayed into the nose, not swallowed.
precautions: Use regularly as directed for best effect, and aim the spray away from the nasal septum to reduce nosebleeds. Tell your doctor of recent nose surgery or injury; long-term use should be monitored.

uses: Used to treat various bacterial infections, including certain chest, throat, ear, skin, and sexually transmitted infections.
sideEffects: May cause diarrhea, nausea, or stomach pain. Rarely it can affect heart rhythm; seek help for fainting, palpitations, or severe diarrhea.
food: Can be taken with or without food; taking with food may reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Complete the full course even though it is often short. Tell your doctor about heart rhythm problems or other medicines, and separate it from antacids by a couple of hours.

uses: Applied to minor cuts, scrapes, and burns to help prevent skin infection.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated; may occasionally cause redness, itching, or a skin allergic reaction at the site.
food: Not applicable — it is applied to the skin, not swallowed.
precautions: For minor external wounds only; stop if a rash or irritation develops. Do not use on large areas, deep or puncture wounds, or for prolonged periods without medical advice.

uses: Used to temporarily numb and relieve pain from sore throats, mouth ulcers, teething, minor skin irritation, or during minor procedures, depending on the product.
sideEffects: May cause temporary stinging, burning, or numbness at the site. Rarely it can cause a serious blood condition (methemoglobinemia) — seek urgent help for bluish lips or skin, shortness of breath, or unusual tiredness.
food: Not applicable — it is used on the skin, mouth, or throat, not swallowed as a tablet.
precautions: Use sparingly and follow the label; oral products are generally not recommended for young children. Avoid eating until mouth or throat numbness wears off to prevent biting or choking.

uses: A skin gel or wash used to treat acne by killing acne-causing bacteria and helping to unclog pores.
sideEffects: Commonly causes dryness, peeling, redness, and mild stinging or burning, especially at first.
food: Not applicable — it is applied to the skin, not swallowed.
precautions: It can bleach hair, towels, and clothing, so let it dry and rinse hands after use. Introduce it gradually, use sunscreen, and avoid the eyes and lips.

uses: Used as a mouthwash, gargle, or spray to relieve pain and inflammation of the mouth and throat, such as a sore throat or mouth ulcers.
sideEffects: May cause temporary stinging or numbness of the mouth; occasionally mild irritation or a dry mouth.
food: Not applicable — it is used in the mouth or throat and then spat out (for rinses), not swallowed.
precautions: For short-term relief; see a doctor if symptoms are severe or persist. Do not exceed the recommended frequency on the label.

uses: Used to calm inflammation, redness, itching, and swelling. It comes in creams and ointments for skin conditions like eczema and dermatitis, and in other forms for inflammatory and allergic conditions.
sideEffects: Skin forms may cause thinning skin, stretch marks, burning, or irritation where applied. Stronger or long-term use can cause more widespread effects; tell your doctor about spreading rash, signs of infection, or worsening skin.
food: Skin creams and ointments are not related to food; if you are given a tablet or liquid form, follow the label, often taken with food to protect the stomach.
precautions: Use only on the areas and for the length of time advised, and avoid the face and broken skin unless told otherwise. Do not stop a long or oral course suddenly, and tell your doctor if you are pregnant.

uses: A combination that reduces inflammation and itching while also treating or preventing bacterial infection. It is used for inflamed skin, eye, or ear conditions where infection is present or likely.
sideEffects: May cause local burning, stinging, itching, or irritation. Allergic reactions to the antibiotic can occur; stop and seek advice if the area becomes more red, swollen, or worsens.
food: Applied to the skin, eye, or ear, so it is not taken with food; follow the label for how to apply.
precautions: Use only for the short course advised, since prolonged use can thin skin, mask infection, or lead to resistance. Tell your doctor if symptoms do not improve or if you have a known neomycin allergy.

uses: An eye drop used to lower raised pressure inside the eye in glaucoma and ocular hypertension, helping protect vision over time.
sideEffects: Commonly causes red eyes, itching, a feeling of something in the eye, and over time may darken the iris, eyelid skin, or lengthen and darken the eyelashes. Some changes may be permanent.
food: Not related to food; it is applied as drops into the eye.
precautions: Remove contact lenses before use and wait before reinserting, and do not let the dropper tip touch the eye. Tell your doctor about other eye drops so doses can be spaced out.

uses: Used for short-term relief of constipation and to empty the bowel before certain medical procedures. It works by stimulating the bowel to move.
sideEffects: May cause stomach cramps, a feeling of urgency, or diarrhea. Overuse can lead to loss of fluids and salts; seek advice if you have severe pain or ongoing symptoms.
food: Tablets are usually taken without food and are often not taken at the same time as milk or antacids; follow the label.
precautions: Use for short periods only, as long-term use can make the bowel dependent on laxatives. Do not use if you have severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting until a cause is known.

uses: An eye drop that lowers raised pressure inside the eye in glaucoma and ocular hypertension. A skin gel form is also used to reduce facial redness.
sideEffects: Eye drops may cause red, dry, or itchy eyes, blurred vision, and drowsiness or dry mouth. Seek advice if you feel very drowsy or dizzy.
food: Not related to food; it is applied as drops into the eye (or as a gel to the skin).
precautions: It can cause drowsiness, so take care with driving until you know how it affects you, and alcohol may add to this. Remove contact lenses before use and space apart from other eye drops.

class: Mucolytic (chest cough medicine that loosens mucus)
uses: Used to thin and loosen thick mucus so that a chesty, productive cough is easier to clear.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; may cause mild stomach upset, nausea, or, rarely, skin rash. Stop and seek help if you get swelling or a severe skin reaction.
food: Usually taken with or after food to reduce the chance of stomach upset; follow the label.
precautions: See a doctor if a cough lasts more than a week, comes back, or is with a high fever. Tell your doctor if you have a stomach ulcer or are pregnant.

uses: Reduces inflammation and is used in inhaler form to control and prevent asthma, as a nasal spray for allergies, and in special oral forms for bowel conditions like Crohn's disease and colitis.
sideEffects: Inhaled or nasal forms may cause throat irritation, hoarseness, nosebleeds, or mouth thrush. Long-term or oral forms can cause more steroid-related effects; report vision changes or frequent infections.
food: The inhaled and nasal forms are not related to food; oral capsules are usually swallowed whole, so follow the label.
precautions: For inhalers, rinse your mouth and spit after use to prevent thrush, and use it regularly for prevention rather than for a sudden attack. Do not stop a regular course suddenly without advice.

uses: An inhaler combining an anti-inflammatory steroid with a long-acting airway opener to control and prevent symptoms of asthma and COPD, such as wheezing and breathlessness.
sideEffects: May cause throat irritation, hoarseness, mouth thrush, headache, tremor, or a fast heartbeat. Seek help if your breathing gets worse or your reliever is needed much more often.
food: Not related to food; it is breathed in as an inhaler.
precautions: Rinse your mouth and spit after each use to help prevent thrush. Some people are prescribed it as a regular preventer only, while others use it both regularly and as a reliever — use it exactly as your doctor directs and do not stop it suddenly without advice.

class: Strong opioid pain reliever / opioid dependence treatment
uses: Used to relieve moderate to severe pain and, in other forms, to treat opioid dependence. It comes as patches, tablets that dissolve under the tongue, and other forms.
sideEffects: Commonly causes drowsiness, constipation, nausea, dizziness, and headache. Serious slowed or shallow breathing can occur; get emergency help for very slow breathing or extreme sleepiness.
food: Under-the-tongue tablets or films are allowed to dissolve and are not swallowed with food or drink; follow the label for your specific form.
precautions: Do not drink alcohol or take other sedatives with it, as this can dangerously slow breathing, and it can affect driving. It carries a risk of dependence, so use exactly as prescribed and do not stop suddenly.

class: Calcium and vitamin D supplement (bone-health supplement)
uses: A supplement combining calcium with vitamin D to support strong bones and to help prevent or treat low calcium or vitamin D, often used in osteoporosis and bone health.
sideEffects: May cause constipation, bloating, gas, or an upset stomach. Very high intake can raise calcium levels; report persistent nausea, excessive thirst, or confusion.
food: Usually taken with or after food, which helps the calcium be absorbed; follow the label.
precautions: Separate it from certain medicines like some antibiotics and thyroid tablets, as it can reduce their absorption. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or a history of kidney stones.

uses: Ear drops used to soften and help remove built-up ear wax. (A similar ingredient is also used in some mouth and teeth products.)
sideEffects: May cause temporary fizzing or bubbling in the ear, mild irritation, or a feeling of fullness. Stop if you get pain, drainage, or bleeding.
food: Not related to food; it is used as drops in the ear.
precautions: Do not use if you have ear pain, discharge, or a possible burst eardrum, or after ear surgery, unless advised. See a doctor if wax problems or hearing changes do not improve.

uses: Lubricating eye drops used to relieve dryness, grittiness, and irritation of the eyes, including dry eye and eye strain.
sideEffects: May cause brief blurred vision after use or mild stinging. Seek advice if eye pain, redness, or vision changes continue.
food: Not related to food; it is applied as drops into the eye.
precautions: Do not let the dropper tip touch the eye or other surfaces to avoid contamination, and follow guidance on contact lenses. See a doctor if symptoms last more than a few days or worsen.

uses: An antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, such as some chest, throat, ear, and urinary tract infections. It does not work against viruses like colds or flu.
sideEffects: Commonly causes diarrhea, nausea, stomach upset, or headache. Seek help for severe or watery diarrhea or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling, or trouble breathing.
food: Can be taken with or without food; taking it with food may reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Finish the full course even if you feel better, and tell your doctor if you have had an allergy to penicillin or cephalosporin antibiotics. Report severe diarrhea, as it can signal a gut infection.

uses: Used to relieve allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny or itchy nose, itchy or watery eyes, and hives or itchy skin.
sideEffects: Generally causes little drowsiness, but some people feel sleepy, and it can cause dry mouth, headache, or tiredness. Seek help for any signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Alcohol may add to any drowsiness, so take care until you know how it affects you, especially with driving. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or are pregnant or breastfeeding.

class: Combination ear preparation (antibiotic + steroid + antifungal + local anesthetic)
uses: A combination product, typically used in the ear, that fights bacterial and fungal infection, reduces inflammation and itching, and eases pain and discomfort.
sideEffects: May cause local stinging, burning, itching, or irritation where applied. Stop and seek advice if the area becomes more red, swollen, or worsens, which may signal an allergic reaction.
food: Not related to food; it is applied locally (usually into the ear) as directed.
precautions: Use only for the short course advised and only in the area directed, since prolonged use can cause problems. Tell your doctor if you have a possible burst eardrum or if symptoms do not improve.

uses: A form of vitamin D used to prevent or treat low vitamin D levels and to support bones, muscles, and the absorption of calcium.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated at normal supplement levels. Very high intake over time can raise calcium too much, causing nausea, constipation, excessive thirst, or weakness.
food: Usually taken with food, ideally a meal containing some fat, which helps absorption; follow the label.
precautions: Do not take more than advised, as vitamin D can build up in the body, and avoid combining several supplements that also contain it. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, high calcium, or take other calcium or vitamin D products.

uses: An antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, such as some urinary, gut, and other infections, and also available as eye and ear drops. It does not work against viral illnesses.
sideEffects: May cause nausea, diarrhea, or dizziness. Less commonly it can cause tendon pain or swelling, nerve tingling, or mood changes; stop and seek advice for tendon pain, severe diarrhea, or a severe reaction.
food: Can be taken with or without food, but avoid taking it at the same time as dairy products, antacids, or calcium/iron supplements, which reduce absorption.
precautions: Avoid strenuous exercise if you notice tendon pain, protect your skin from strong sunlight, and stay well hydrated. Tell your doctor about heart-rhythm problems and other medicines, as interactions are possible; finish the full course.

uses: An antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, including some skin, dental, and other infections, and available as a topical form for acne. It does not treat viral illnesses.
sideEffects: Commonly causes nausea, stomach upset, or diarrhea; topical forms may cause dryness or irritation. Report severe, watery, or bloody diarrhea, which can occur during or after treatment and needs prompt attention.
food: Oral capsules are usually taken with a full glass of water, and may be taken with food to reduce stomach upset; follow the label.
precautions: Do not ignore significant diarrhea, as it can signal a serious gut infection, and contact your doctor promptly. Finish the full course and tell your doctor about any past bowel problems.

class: Very strong topical corticosteroid (anti-inflammatory skin steroid)
uses: A potent steroid cream or ointment used for short-term treatment of severe or stubborn inflammatory skin conditions such as psoriasis and eczema that have not responded to milder steroids.
sideEffects: May cause thinning skin, stretch marks, burning, stinging, or changes in skin color where applied. Because it is strong, longer use raises the risk of wider steroid effects; report worsening or infected skin.
food: Applied to the skin, so it is not related to food; follow the label for how and where to apply.
precautions: Use only thin amounts on the areas advised, for the short time directed, and generally avoid the face, groin, and broken skin unless told otherwise. Do not stop a longer course abruptly, and tell your doctor if you are pregnant.

uses: Used to help control certain types of seizures and to treat panic and some anxiety conditions. It works by calming overactivity in the brain and nerves.
sideEffects: Commonly causes drowsiness, dizziness, tiredness, poor coordination, and sometimes memory or mood changes. Seek help for very slow or shallow breathing or extreme sleepiness.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not drink alcohol or combine with other sedatives, and take care with driving as it causes drowsiness. It can cause dependence, so use exactly as prescribed and do not stop suddenly, since abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal or seizures.

uses: Helps prevent blood clots by stopping platelets from sticking together. Commonly used after a heart attack, stroke, or certain heart-artery procedures (like stents), or in people with peripheral artery disease.
sideEffects: Easier bruising and bleeding are common; less often, stomach upset or rash. Seek help urgently for unusual or heavy bleeding, black/tarry stools, or blood in urine or vomit.
food: Can be taken with or without food; taking it with food may ease stomach upset.
precautions: Increases bleeding risk, so tell any doctor or dentist you take it before procedures, and do not stop suddenly without medical advice as this can raise clot risk. Use caution combining it with other blood thinners, aspirin, or certain acid-reducers, and mention all your medicines to your pharmacist.

uses: Treats fungal and yeast infections of the skin or vaginal area, such as athlete's foot, ringworm, and thrush. Usually applied as a cream, or used as a pessary/vaginal tablet.
sideEffects: Mild burning, stinging, itching, or redness at the site of use can occur. Stop and seek advice if you get a severe rash, swelling, or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Applied to the skin or used vaginally, so food does not matter; follow the label.
precautions: For external or vaginal use only unless told otherwise — avoid getting it in the eyes. Tell your doctor if symptoms do not improve, keep coming back, or if you are pregnant.

uses: A combined skin cream in which the antifungal clears fungal or yeast infection while the steroid reduces inflammation, redness, and itching. Used for itchy, inflamed fungal skin conditions.
sideEffects: Local burning, stinging, dryness, or irritation may occur. With prolonged use the steroid can thin the skin or cause other skin changes, so let your doctor know if the skin worsens.
food: Applied to the skin, so food does not matter; follow the label.
precautions: Meant for short-term use on affected skin only — avoid the face, broken skin, and long-term use unless directed, and do not cover with airtight dressings unless advised. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or the rash does not improve.

uses: Lowers blood sugar in type 2 diabetes by making the kidneys remove excess sugar through the urine. It is also used to protect the heart and kidneys in certain people, including some with heart failure or chronic kidney disease.
sideEffects: Genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, and increased urination are common. Rarely it can cause a serious condition called diabetic ketoacidosis — seek urgent help for nausea, vomiting, belly pain, fast breathing, or unusual tiredness.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Drink enough fluids and be alert for dehydration or dizziness, especially if you are unwell, not eating, or having surgery, when it may need to be paused. Tell your doctor about kidney problems, and note it may cause low blood sugar if combined with insulin or certain other diabetes medicines.

uses: Relieves a dry, tickly cough that has no phlegm by calming the cough reflex. Often found in over-the-counter cough remedies.
sideEffects: May cause mild drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, or stomach upset. These are usually mild.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Not for coughs that bring up phlegm, and check with a pharmacist before combining it with other cough-and-cold products to avoid doubling up. Avoid alcohol, and do not use with or soon after antidepressants known as MAO inhibitors — tell your doctor about your other medicines.

uses: A combined cold-and-flu remedy that eases a dry cough, unblocks a stuffy nose, and dries up a runny nose and sneezing. Used for short-term relief of cough and cold symptoms.
sideEffects: Drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and a faster or pounding heartbeat can occur; the decongestant may cause restlessness or raise blood pressure. The antihistamine part often causes sleepiness.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: It can make you drowsy, so avoid alcohol and do not drive until you know how it affects you. Use caution if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, or prostate problems, and avoid taking other cold products at the same time to prevent overdosing on the same ingredients.

uses: Relieves pain, swelling, and inflammation from conditions such as arthritis, muscle or joint injuries, and other painful conditions. Available as tablets, gels, and other forms.
sideEffects: Stomach upset, indigestion, heartburn, and nausea are common. It can rarely cause stomach ulcers or bleeding — seek help for severe stomach pain, black stools, or vomiting blood.
food: Oral forms are best taken with or just after food to protect the stomach.
precautions: Long-term or high use may raise the risk of stomach, heart, or kidney problems, so use the lowest amount for the shortest time. Avoid or use with caution if you have ulcers, heart or kidney disease, or are pregnant, and avoid combining with other NSAIDs or excess alcohol.

uses: A rub-on product combining an anti-inflammatory with warming/cooling ingredients to relieve local muscle and joint pain, sprains, strains, and backache.
sideEffects: Skin irritation, redness, burning, or itching at the application site can occur. Stop use if you get a severe rash or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Applied to the skin, so food does not matter; follow the label.
precautions: For external use only on intact skin — avoid broken skin, eyes, and mouth, and wash your hands after applying. Do not cover with a tight bandage or apply heat over it, and use caution if you are sensitive to aspirin-type medicines or are pregnant.

uses: A combined cough syrup that helps loosen and clear mucus while the antihistamine eases an associated runny nose or allergy-type cough. Used for short-term relief of cough with congestion.
sideEffects: Drowsiness and dry mouth are common because of the antihistamine; some people feel dizzy or have mild stomach upset.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: It commonly causes drowsiness, so avoid alcohol and do not drive until you know how it affects you. Use caution with other sedating medicines, and check with a pharmacist if you have breathing problems, glaucoma, or prostate issues.

uses: Relieves nausea and vomiting and helps the stomach empty, easing bloating, fullness, and reflux-type discomfort. Sometimes used for nausea linked to other conditions or medicines.
sideEffects: Dry mouth, headache, or mild stomach cramps can occur. Rarely it can affect the heart's rhythm — seek help for fainting, palpitations, or an irregular heartbeat.
food: Usually taken before meals so it can work as the stomach empties; follow the label.
precautions: Because of a small risk of heart-rhythm changes, it is generally used at the lowest amount for the shortest time and avoided in people with certain heart problems. Tell your doctor about heart or liver conditions and all other medicines you take, as some interact with it.

class: Glaucoma eye drops (combination to lower eye pressure)
uses: Combined eye drops that lower raised pressure inside the eye in glaucoma or ocular hypertension by reducing the amount of fluid the eye makes.
sideEffects: Temporary stinging, burning, blurred vision, a bitter taste, or red or watery eyes are common. Because a small amount can be absorbed, it can occasionally cause a slow heartbeat or breathing changes.
food: It is an eye drop, so food does not apply; use as directed on the label.
precautions: Press gently on the inner corner of the eye after use to limit body-wide absorption, and remove contact lenses before applying. Tell your doctor if you have asthma, breathing problems, heart conditions, or a sulfa allergy, and do not stop suddenly without advice.

uses: Treats a wide range of bacterial infections, including chest, skin, and urinary infections, and some sexually transmitted infections; it is also used for acne and to help prevent malaria.
sideEffects: Nausea, stomach upset, and diarrhea are common, and it can make skin more sensitive to sunlight. Seek help for severe or bloody diarrhea, painful swallowing, or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Can be taken with food to reduce stomach upset, but take it with plenty of water and stay upright afterward to avoid throat irritation.
precautions: Avoid taking it at the same time as dairy, antacids, or iron/calcium supplements, which reduce its effect. Use sun protection, finish the full course, and avoid in pregnancy and in young children as it can affect developing teeth and bones.

uses: Prevents and treats blood clots, such as clots in the legs or lungs, and is used around surgery or during certain heart conditions. Given as an injection under the skin.
sideEffects: Bruising, pain, or small lumps at the injection site and easier bleeding are common. Seek urgent help for heavy or unusual bleeding, black stools, or blood in urine or vomit.
food: It is an injection, so it is not affected by food.
precautions: It raises bleeding risk, so tell any doctor or dentist you use it and report unusual bleeding promptly. Do not combine with other blood thinners unless directed, use caution with kidney problems, and follow instructions carefully for safe injection and needle disposal.

uses: Used to treat depression and anxiety disorders by helping to balance a brain chemical called serotonin. It often takes a few weeks to reach its full effect.
sideEffects: Nausea, headache, sleep changes, dry mouth, and sexual side effects are common, especially early on. Contact your doctor if mood worsens or you have thoughts of self-harm, particularly in the first weeks.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not stop suddenly, as this can cause withdrawal-type symptoms — reduce gradually with medical guidance. Limit alcohol, and tell your doctor about other medicines (especially other antidepressants or triptans) because of a rare serious reaction called serotonin syndrome.

uses: Reduces stomach acid to relieve heartburn and acid reflux, and to help heal or prevent ulcers and inflammation of the food pipe. Also used alongside antibiotics to treat H. pylori infection.
sideEffects: Headache, diarrhea, constipation, wind, or stomach pain can occur and are usually mild. Long-term use may affect the absorption of some nutrients.
food: Usually taken before a meal, often in the morning; follow the label.
precautions: Long-term use is linked to possible effects on magnesium, vitamin B12, and bone strength, so use it only as long as needed. Tell your doctor if heartburn persists or you have difficulty swallowing, and mention other medicines as it can affect some (for example certain blood thinners).

uses: Relieves pain and inflammation in conditions such as arthritis and gout, and can be used for short-term pain. It is designed to be somewhat gentler on the stomach than older NSAIDs.
sideEffects: It can raise blood pressure and cause swelling of the ankles, dizziness, or stomach upset. Seek help for chest pain, severe stomach pain, or black stools.
food: Can be taken with or without food; it may work faster on an empty stomach.
precautions: It may increase the risk of heart, blood-pressure, and kidney problems, so it is avoided in uncontrolled high blood pressure and some heart conditions and used at the lowest amount for the shortest time. Tell your doctor about heart, kidney, or stomach problems and avoid combining with other NSAIDs.

uses: Treats severe pain, such as ongoing cancer pain or pain not controlled by weaker painkillers. It comes in forms like skin patches and other specialist preparations.
sideEffects: Constipation, drowsiness, nausea, and confusion are common. Serious slowed or shallow breathing can occur — seek emergency help for very slow breathing, extreme sleepiness, or unresponsiveness.
food: Depends on the form; follow the exact instructions on the label or from your doctor.
precautions: It is a powerful, potentially addictive medicine that can dangerously slow breathing, especially with alcohol, sedatives, or sleep medicines, which must be avoided unless a doctor advises. Never exceed the prescribed amount, do not stop abruptly after regular use, and store it securely away from children and others — used patches still contain medicine and must be disposed of safely.

uses: Relieves allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny or itchy nose, itchy or watery eyes, and hives. It is a non-drowsy type of antihistamine for most people.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; some people get headache, dry mouth, nausea, or mild drowsiness.
food: Best taken with water and not with fruit juices (like orange, apple, or grapefruit), which can reduce how well it works.
precautions: Avoid taking it at the same time as antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium, which can lower its effect. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or if symptoms do not improve.

uses: Treats fungal and yeast infections such as vaginal or oral thrush and some other internal fungal infections, and can be used to help prevent them in certain people.
sideEffects: Nausea, stomach upset, headache, or diarrhea can occur. Seek help for a severe skin rash, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or signs of liver trouble.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: It interacts with many medicines, so tell your pharmacist everything you take, and mention any liver problems or heart-rhythm conditions. Let your doctor know if you are pregnant, as it is generally avoided in pregnancy except when clearly needed.

uses: Used for depression, some anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders, and certain other conditions by helping to balance the brain chemical serotonin. It usually takes a few weeks to work fully.
sideEffects: Nausea, headache, difficulty sleeping, restlessness, reduced appetite, and sexual side effects are common early on. Contact your doctor if mood worsens or you have thoughts of self-harm, especially in the first weeks.
food: Can be taken with or without food; taking it earlier in the day may help if it disturbs sleep.
precautions: Do not stop suddenly without advice, and be aware it stays in the body a long time. Limit alcohol and tell your doctor about other medicines (especially other antidepressants, triptans, or blood thinners) because of interaction risks including a rare serious reaction called serotonin syndrome.

class: Steroid (corticosteroid) — usually a nasal spray or inhaler
uses: Used to reduce inflammation and swelling, commonly to control nasal allergy symptoms (sneezing, stuffy or runny nose) or, in inhaler form, to prevent asthma symptoms.
sideEffects: May cause nasal dryness, irritation, or nosebleeds; the inhaler can cause hoarseness or mouth thrush. Seek help for vision changes or signs of a serious allergic reaction.
food: Not related to food — it is sprayed in the nose or breathed in; follow the label.
precautions: Works best when used regularly, not just when symptoms flare. Rinse your mouth after using the inhaler, and tell your doctor about long-term use or recent infections.

uses: Used to prevent or treat low folate levels and is commonly taken before and during pregnancy to support healthy development of the baby.
sideEffects: Usually very well tolerated; occasionally mild stomach upset or a bad taste. Serious reactions are rare.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Tell your doctor if you have vitamin B12 deficiency or anemia, as folic acid can mask it. Some seizure and other medicines can interact.

class: Antibiotic (aminoglycoside), used on the skin, in the eye, or in the ear
uses: Used to treat or prevent bacterial infections of the skin, eyes, or ears.
sideEffects: May cause local stinging, itching, or irritation where applied. Stop and seek advice if you develop a rash or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Not related to food — it is applied to the affected area; follow the label.
precautions: Use only for the length of time directed, as prolonged use can lead to further irritation or resistance. Do not use in the ear if the eardrum may be perforated unless told to.

uses: Used to remove excess fluid from the body in conditions like heart failure, or liver or kidney problems, and sometimes to help lower blood pressure.
sideEffects: Increases urination and can cause dizziness, dehydration, and low potassium or other salt imbalances. Seek help for muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat, or fainting.
food: Can be taken with or without food; often taken in the morning to avoid getting up at night to urinate.
precautions: Your doctor may check your kidneys and blood salts periodically. Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness, and tell your doctor about other blood-pressure or heart medicines.

class: Antibiotic (often a skin cream or eye drops/gel)
uses: Used to treat bacterial infections, most commonly of the skin (such as impetigo) or the eyes.
sideEffects: May cause mild stinging, redness, or irritation at the site. Stop and seek advice if you get a rash or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: The topical forms are not related to food; if taken by mouth it is usually taken with food — follow the label.
precautions: Finish the full course as directed even if you feel better, and avoid overuse to reduce the chance of resistance.

uses: Used to relieve certain types of nerve pain and to help control some seizures; it is also sometimes used for restless legs.
sideEffects: Commonly causes drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, or mild swelling of the legs. Seek urgent help for mood changes, thoughts of self-harm, or trouble breathing.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not stop suddenly, as this can trigger seizures or withdrawal; your doctor will taper it. Avoid alcohol, take care when driving, and be cautious combining it with other sedating medicines.

uses: Used to treat bacterial eye infections such as conjunctivitis (pink eye).
sideEffects: May cause temporary eye stinging, irritation, redness, or blurred vision. Stop and seek advice if you get worsening pain or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Not related to food — it is used in the eye; follow the label.
precautions: Do not wear contact lenses while you have the infection unless told otherwise, and avoid touching the dropper tip to your eye to prevent contamination.

uses: Used to lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes by helping the body release more insulin, alongside diet and exercise.
sideEffects: Can cause low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) and some weight gain. Treat low blood sugar promptly and seek help if it is severe.
food: Usually taken with breakfast or the first main meal of the day.
precautions: The risk of low blood sugar rises if you skip meals, exercise more than usual, or drink alcohol. Learn to recognize and treat low-sugar symptoms.

uses: Used to replace fluids and body salts lost through diarrhea, vomiting, or other causes of dehydration.
sideEffects: Generally very safe; drinking it too quickly may cause mild nausea or vomiting.
food: Can be taken at any time; sip slowly and follow the mixing instructions on the label.
precautions: Mix with the correct amount of clean water and do not add extra sugar or salt. Seek medical care if there are signs of severe dehydration, blood in stool, or symptoms that do not improve.

uses: Commonly used as a suppository or enema to relieve occasional constipation by drawing water into the bowel; also used as a skin or lip moisturizer.
sideEffects: May cause mild rectal irritation, burning, or cramping when used for constipation.
food: Not related to food; follow the label.
precautions: Intended for short-term, occasional use. See a doctor if constipation is ongoing or if you notice rectal bleeding.

uses: Used to loosen and thin mucus so that a chesty, congested cough is easier to clear.
sideEffects: Usually mild; may cause slight nausea, dizziness, or drowsiness.
food: Can be taken with or without food; drink plenty of water to help it work.
precautions: See a doctor if the cough lasts more than about a week, keeps coming back, or comes with fever. Check combination cold products so you do not double up on ingredients.

uses: Used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots, such as in the legs or lungs, and in certain medical or surgical situations.
sideEffects: The main risk is bleeding and easy bruising. Seek urgent help for unusual or heavy bleeding, black stools, or a serious allergic reaction.
food: Not related to food — it is given by injection.
precautions: Tell all your healthcare providers you are on a blood thinner, and report unusual bleeding. Many medicines, including aspirin and other pain relievers, can increase bleeding risk.

uses: Used to reduce inflammation, redness, and itching; the cream treats skin conditions like eczema and rashes, while tablets or injections treat a range of inflammatory conditions.
sideEffects: The cream may cause skin thinning or irritation with prolonged use; tablets over time can raise blood sugar, affect mood, or weaken bones.
food: The cream is not related to food; tablets are usually taken with food to protect the stomach.
precautions: Use the cream thinly and for the shortest time needed, avoiding the face unless directed. Do not stop steroid tablets abruptly, as they must be tapered under medical guidance.

uses: Used to relieve dryness, irritation, and grittiness in the eyes.
sideEffects: May cause brief blurred vision or mild stinging right after use.
food: Not related to food — it is used in the eye.
precautions: Avoid touching the dropper tip to your eye or any surface. Remove contact lenses before use unless the product says it is contact-lens friendly.

class: Pain reliever, fever reducer, and anti-inflammatory (NSAID)
uses: Used to relieve pain such as headache, muscle or period pain, to reduce fever, and to ease inflammation.
sideEffects: Can cause stomach upset, heartburn, or, especially with long-term use, stomach ulcers or bleeding. Seek help for black stools, vomiting blood, or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Best taken with food or milk to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Use caution if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, heart disease, or asthma, and avoid combining with other NSAIDs. Limit alcohol, and avoid in late pregnancy unless a doctor advises.

class: Combination pain reliever and fever reducer (NSAID plus paracetamol)
uses: A single product combining two pain relievers to ease pain and reduce fever, often used when one alone is not enough.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset or heartburn from the ibuprofen part. Seek help for black stools, vomiting blood, or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Best taken with food to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Do not take other products containing ibuprofen or paracetamol at the same time, to avoid overdose. Use caution with stomach, kidney, heart, or liver problems and limit alcohol.

uses: Used to control blood sugar in diabetes, taken around mealtimes to handle the rise in sugar after eating.
sideEffects: The main risk is low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion); injection sites may become red or lumpy. Treat low sugar promptly and get help if it is severe.
food: Given just before or right after a meal because it acts quickly.
precautions: Do not skip a meal after taking it, and learn to recognize and treat low blood sugar. Rotate injection sites and store insulin as directed.

uses: Used to provide steady background blood-sugar control in diabetes over roughly a full day.
sideEffects: Can cause low blood sugar, some weight gain, and injection-site reactions. Treat low sugar promptly and get help if it is severe.
food: Usually given once a day at the same time, with or without regard to meals.
precautions: Take it at a consistent time each day and do not mix it with other insulins in the same syringe unless told to. Learn to recognize and treat low blood sugar.

uses: Used to provide longer-lasting blood-sugar control in diabetes, often once or twice daily.
sideEffects: Can cause low blood sugar, weight gain, and injection-site reactions. Treat low sugar promptly and get help if it is severe.
food: Timed in relation to meals according to your treatment plan — follow your prescriber's instructions.
precautions: This is a cloudy insulin that should be gently rolled to mix before use, not shaken. Keep timing consistent, and learn to recognize and treat low blood sugar.

uses: A premixed insulin used to control blood sugar in diabetes with fewer separate injections, covering both mealtime and background needs.
sideEffects: Can cause low blood sugar, weight gain, and injection-site reactions. Treat low sugar promptly and get help if it is severe.
food: Usually given before a meal — follow your prescriber's instructions on timing.
precautions: Gently roll the cloudy mixture to blend it before injecting, and eat on schedule after your dose. Keep timing consistent and learn to recognize and treat low blood sugar.

uses: Used to control blood sugar in people with diabetes. It works quickly, so it is usually given around mealtimes to cover the rise in blood sugar after eating.
sideEffects: The main risk is low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion) — treat promptly with fast sugar and seek help if severe. Injection-site redness, lumps, and some weight gain can also occur.
food: Taken shortly before or just after a meal, since it acts quickly — do not take it without eating.
precautions: Carry a source of fast sugar and know the signs of low blood sugar; rotate injection sites, never share pens or needles, and do not skip meals after dosing.

uses: Used to control blood sugar in people with diabetes. It is a short-acting insulin usually given before meals to manage the after-meal blood-sugar rise.
sideEffects: Low blood sugar is the main concern (sweating, trembling, hunger, confusion) — treat quickly and get help if severe. Injection-site reactions and weight gain may also occur.
food: Usually taken a little before a meal so its effect matches your food — follow your prescriber's timing.
precautions: Learn to recognize and treat low blood sugar, carry fast sugar, rotate injection sites, and never share pens or needles.

uses: A short-acting soluble insulin used to control blood sugar in diabetes, generally given before meals. It can also be used in medical settings to manage high blood sugar.
sideEffects: Low blood sugar is the main risk (shakiness, sweating, confusion) — treat promptly and seek help if severe. Injection-site reactions and weight gain can occur.
food: Usually given a short time before eating so its action matches your meal — follow the prescribed timing.
precautions: Recognize and be ready to treat low blood sugar, keep fast sugar handy, rotate injection sites, and do not share injection devices.

uses: An inhaled medicine that relaxes and opens the airways, used mainly for long-term breathing conditions such as COPD and sometimes asthma to ease wheezing and breathlessness.
sideEffects: Commonly causes dry mouth, throat irritation, and cough. Getting the spray in the eyes can cause temporary blurred vision or eye discomfort.
food: It is inhaled, so it is not related to food — use it as directed on the label.
precautions: It is not a fast-acting rescue inhaler for sudden severe attacks; avoid spraying it into the eyes, and tell your doctor if you have glaucoma or prostate/urinary problems.

uses: An inhaled combination that opens the airways in two ways, used for breathing conditions such as COPD and asthma to relieve wheezing and shortness of breath.
sideEffects: May cause tremor (shaky hands), faster heartbeat, headache, and dry mouth. Getting the spray in the eyes can cause temporary blurred vision.
food: It is inhaled and not related to food — use it exactly as directed on the label.
precautions: Tell your doctor if you have heart problems, an overactive thyroid, or glaucoma; avoid getting it in the eyes and do not use more than prescribed.

uses: A natural fiber used to relieve constipation and keep bowel movements regular, and sometimes to help with irritable bowel symptoms or to support healthy cholesterol levels.
sideEffects: Can cause bloating, gas, and mild stomach cramps, which often settle as your body adjusts.
food: Can be taken with or without food, but always mix it with and follow it by plenty of water.
precautions: Drink enough fluid to avoid choking or bowel blockage; do not use if you have a bowel obstruction, and take it a couple of hours apart from other medicines since it can reduce their absorption.

uses: Treats fungal infections. It is widely used on the skin and as a shampoo for fungal skin conditions and dandruff; the tablet form is reserved for limited situations because of liver risk.
sideEffects: Creams and shampoos may cause skin irritation, itching, or dryness. The tablet form can cause nausea and, importantly, liver problems.
food: Skin creams and shampoos follow the label. If prescribed as tablets, they are usually taken with food.
precautions: The tablet form can harm the liver and interacts with many medicines and alcohol — use only under close medical supervision and report yellowing skin/eyes, dark urine, or severe tiredness.

uses: Used to relieve pain, swelling, and inflammation, such as in arthritis, muscle and joint injuries, and general aches.
sideEffects: Can cause stomach upset, heartburn, and, less commonly, stomach ulcers or bleeding and kidney problems. Seek help for black stools, vomiting blood, or severe stomach pain.
food: Take with food or milk to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Long-term use, alcohol, and older age raise the risk of stomach bleeding; use caution if you have kidney, heart, or ulcer problems, and avoid in late pregnancy.

uses: A potent anti-inflammatory painkiller used for short-term relief of moderate to severe pain, often after surgery or injury.
sideEffects: Carries a notable risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding and of kidney problems. Seek help for black stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or reduced urination.
food: Take with food or milk to lessen stomach irritation.
precautions: Meant only for short-term use; do not combine with other NSAIDs, limit alcohol, and use with caution if you have kidney, heart, ulcer, or bleeding problems.

uses: Used to relieve allergy symptoms. As eye drops it eases itchy, watery, allergic eyes; the oral form is used for allergic conditions and to help prevent asthma symptoms over time.
sideEffects: The oral form can cause drowsiness, increased appetite, and dry mouth. Eye drops may cause brief stinging or mild eye irritation.
food: The oral form can be taken with or without food; taking it with food may reduce stomach upset — follow the label.
precautions: May cause drowsiness, so be cautious driving or using machines and limit alcohol; the oral form prevents symptoms and is not for immediate relief of a sudden asthma attack.

class: Eye-pressure lowering drops for glaucoma (prostaglandin analog)
uses: Eye drops used to lower raised pressure inside the eye in glaucoma or ocular hypertension, helping protect vision over time.
sideEffects: May cause eye redness, stinging, a feeling of something in the eye, gradual darkening of the iris or eyelid skin, and longer, darker eyelashes.
food: It is an eye drop and is not related to food.
precautions: Usually used once each evening at the same time; remove contact lenses before use and wait before reinserting, and avoid touching the dropper tip to the eye or fingers.

uses: Used to help prevent and control seizures in people with epilepsy, often alongside other seizure medicines.
sideEffects: Commonly causes drowsiness, dizziness, and tiredness. It can also cause mood or behavior changes such as irritability, anxiety, or low mood — report these to your doctor.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not stop suddenly, as this can trigger seizures; tell your doctor about any mood changes or thoughts of self-harm, and be cautious driving until you know how it affects you.

uses: Used to relieve allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny or itchy nose, watery eyes, and hives or itching.
sideEffects: May cause drowsiness, tiredness, or dry mouth, though it is less sedating than older antihistamines.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Alcohol and other sedating medicines can increase drowsiness; use caution when driving until you know how it affects you.

uses: An antibiotic used to treat a range of bacterial infections, including certain chest, urinary, sinus, and skin infections.
sideEffects: May cause nausea, diarrhea, and dizziness. Less commonly it can cause tendon pain or rupture, nerve problems (numbness/tingling), and mood changes — seek help if these occur.
food: Can be taken with or without food, with plenty of water; keep it separated from dairy, antacids, and iron/calcium/zinc supplements, which reduce its absorption.
precautions: Tendon and nerve problems are more likely in older people and those on steroids; avoid excessive sun exposure, finish the full course, and report tendon pain, tingling, or mood changes promptly.

uses: Opens up narrowed airways to relieve wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath in asthma and other breathing conditions.
sideEffects: May cause tremor (shaky hands), faster heartbeat, headache, and feeling nervous or restless.
food: When inhaled it is not related to food; any oral form can be taken with or without food — follow the label.
precautions: Tell your doctor if you need it more often than usual, as this may mean your breathing condition is worsening; use with caution if you have heart problems or an overactive thyroid.

class: Cough medicine combination (bronchodilator + mucus thinner + expectorant)
uses: A combination used for coughs with chest tightness and thick mucus — it helps open the airways and loosen and clear phlegm.
sideEffects: May cause tremor, faster heartbeat, nausea, or stomach upset.
food: Often taken with food to reduce stomach upset — follow the label.
precautions: It is meant for a chesty, productive cough rather than a dry cough; use with caution if you have heart problems or an overactive thyroid, and do not exceed the recommended amount.

uses: Replaces thyroid hormone in people with an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) to restore normal energy, metabolism, and body function.
sideEffects: At the right dose there are usually few side effects; too much can cause a fast or pounding heartbeat, weight loss, tremor, sweating, and trouble sleeping — report these.
food: Best taken on an empty stomach, usually in the morning, some time before food, and kept apart from certain supplements.
precautions: Take it consistently and do not stop without advice; separate it from calcium, iron, and antacids, and tell your doctor before switching brands as this can affect your levels.

uses: Used to lower high blood pressure and to protect the kidneys, particularly in people with diabetes, and it may be used in certain heart conditions.
sideEffects: May cause dizziness (especially with the first doses) and, less commonly, raised potassium levels. It is generally well tolerated.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Should not be used in pregnancy; be cautious with potassium supplements or salt substitutes, and stand up slowly if you feel dizzy.

uses: Used to relieve constipation by drawing water into the bowel to soften stools and make them easier to pass.
sideEffects: May cause bloating, gas, mild stomach cramps, or nausea; taking too much can cause diarrhea.
food: Dissolved in water and can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Drink plenty of fluids while using it; do not use if you have a suspected bowel blockage, and tell your doctor if constipation persists or you have ongoing stomach pain.

uses: A combination laxative used for constipation — one part draws water into the bowel while the other lubricates the stool to ease passage.
sideEffects: May cause loose stools, stomach cramps, or leakage of oily fluid from the back passage.
food: Follow the label for timing; avoid taking it right at bedtime while lying down.
precautions: Long-term use of the paraffin part can reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; avoid taking it lying down (risk of it entering the lungs), and use with caution if you have kidney problems because of the magnesium.

uses: Commonly used for short-term relief of mild-to-moderate pain, including period (menstrual) pain, headache, dental pain, and muscle or joint aches. It also helps reduce inflammation and fever.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset, indigestion, nausea, or diarrhea. Seek help promptly if you notice black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash or swelling.
food: Best taken with food or milk to reduce the chance of stomach irritation.
precautions: Use for the shortest time needed; avoid heavy alcohol use. Tell your doctor if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, heart disease, or asthma, and use caution in pregnancy.

uses: A combination used mainly for painful cramping, especially period (menstrual) pain and abdominal cramps. The NSAID part eases pain and inflammation while the antispasmodic relaxes cramping muscle in the gut and uterus.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset or nausea from the NSAID, plus dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, or drowsiness from the antispasmodic. Seek help for black or bloody stools, severe stomach pain, or a fast heartbeat.
food: Usually taken with food to lessen stomach irritation.
precautions: Avoid driving until you know how it affects you, and limit alcohol. Use caution if you have glaucoma, urinary or bowel blockage, stomach ulcers, or kidney or heart problems; check with your doctor in pregnancy.

uses: Used topically for a cooling, soothing effect to ease minor muscle and joint aches, and in lozenges or rubs to relieve itching, minor throat irritation, or a blocked-feeling nose.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; may cause mild skin redness, burning, stinging, or a rash where applied. Stop use if irritation is strong or persistent.
food: Not applicable for creams, rubs, or patches; for lozenges, simply follow the label.
precautions: For external or oral-lozenge use as directed only — do not swallow rubs or apply to broken, irritated skin, and keep away from the eyes. Avoid heat or tight bandaging over treated skin.

uses: Used to control blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, usually alongside diet and exercise. It helps the body respond better to insulin and lowers the amount of sugar made by the liver.
sideEffects: Commonly causes nausea, diarrhea, gas, or a metallic taste, which often ease over time. Rarely it can cause a serious build-up of acid (lactic acidosis); seek urgent care for unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, extreme tiredness, or feeling very cold.
food: Take with or right after food to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Limit alcohol, and tell your doctor about kidney or liver problems. It may be paused around surgery or scans that use contrast dye; long-term use can lower vitamin B12.

uses: A form of vitamin B12 used to treat or prevent B12 deficiency and to support nerve health; it is often used for tingling or nerve-related discomfort linked to low B12.
sideEffects: Generally very well tolerated; mild side effects such as nausea, headache, or occasional injection-site soreness can occur. Allergic reactions are rare.
food: Can usually be taken with or without food; follow the label.
precautions: Let your doctor know your full medical history so the cause of any deficiency is checked. Tell your provider about all supplements you take to avoid unnecessary duplication.

uses: Used to lower high blood pressure, ease chest pain (angina), steady an irregular or fast heartbeat, and protect the heart after a heart attack or in heart failure.
sideEffects: May cause tiredness, dizziness, slow heartbeat, or cold hands and feet. Seek help for fainting, very slow pulse, shortness of breath, or swelling of the legs.
food: Often taken with or just after food, which can help absorption; follow the label consistently.
precautions: Do not stop suddenly, as this can worsen heart problems — your doctor will lower the dose gradually. Use caution if you have asthma, certain heart-rhythm conditions, or diabetes, since it can mask low-blood-sugar warning signs.

uses: Used to treat certain bacterial infections and parasitic (protozoal) infections, including some dental, gut, and gynecological infections. It works against germs that grow without oxygen.
sideEffects: Common effects include nausea, metallic taste, headache, and loss of appetite. Seek help for numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, seizures, or severe diarrhea.
food: Take with food or a full glass of water to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: Avoid alcohol during treatment and for a couple of days after, as the combination can cause flushing, nausea, and a fast heartbeat. Finish the full course even if you feel better, and tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.

uses: Used to treat fungal and yeast infections of the skin, nails, mouth, or vagina, such as athlete's foot, ringworm, and thrush, depending on the product form.
sideEffects: Topical forms may cause mild burning, itching, or redness where applied; oral gel can cause an altered taste or mild nausea. Stop and seek help if you get strong irritation or an allergic reaction.
food: Not applicable for skin creams or vaginal products; for oral gel, follow the label (often kept in the mouth after food).
precautions: Use for the full recommended course to fully clear the infection. Keep creams and vaginal products away from the eyes, and tell your doctor about other medicines, as some interactions can occur.

uses: A corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation. Depending on the form it treats hay fever and nasal allergy symptoms, helps prevent asthma attacks, or calms inflamed, itchy skin conditions.
sideEffects: Nasal sprays may cause nose irritation, dryness, or nosebleeds; inhalers can cause throat irritation or mouth thrush; skin creams may cause local thinning or irritation with prolonged use. Report persistent nosebleeds or vision changes.
food: Not applicable — it is applied to the nose, lungs, or skin rather than swallowed; follow the label for the specific product.
precautions: Use regularly as directed, since preventer effects build up over time, and rinse your mouth after inhaler use. Avoid overusing skin forms on large areas or thin skin, and tell your doctor about recent infections.

uses: Used to help prevent asthma symptoms and to relieve ongoing hay fever and allergy symptoms. It is a long-term controller, not a rescue medicine for a sudden asthma attack.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated; may cause headache, stomach upset, or vivid dreams. Importantly, it can cause mood or behavior changes such as anxiety, low mood, or sleep problems — tell your doctor promptly if these occur.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Keep using your regular asthma inhalers and do not rely on this for sudden attacks. Because of possible mood or behavior effects, watch for changes in yourself or a child and report them.

uses: A combination used for allergy symptoms such as runny or blocked nose, sneezing, and itching, often when both a leukotriene blocker and an antihistamine are helpful together.
sideEffects: May cause drowsiness, dry mouth, headache, or stomach upset. As with montelukast alone, watch for mood or behavior changes such as anxiety or low mood and report them.
food: Can generally be taken with or without food; follow the label.
precautions: May cause drowsiness, so be careful driving or operating machinery and limit alcohol. Keep using rescue inhalers for asthma, and tell your doctor about kidney problems or any mood changes.

uses: Used to treat certain bacterial infections such as some chest, sinus, and skin infections; an eye-drop form treats bacterial eye infections. It does not work against viruses like colds or flu.
sideEffects: May cause nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, or headache; eye drops may cause brief stinging. Seek help for tendon pain or swelling, unusual nerve symptoms, palpitations, or severe diarrhea.
food: Tablets can be taken with or without food, but avoid taking them at the same time as dairy, antacids, or iron/zinc products, which reduce absorption.
precautions: Fluoroquinolones carry a risk of tendon, nerve, and heart-rhythm problems — stop and seek care if you get sudden tendon pain, tingling, or fainting. Complete the full course and tell your doctor about heart-rhythm conditions or other medicines.

uses: An antibiotic ointment or cream applied to the skin to treat minor bacterial skin infections such as impetigo and infected cuts or sores.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; may cause mild burning, stinging, itching, or redness where applied. Stop and seek advice if irritation is strong or a rash develops.
food: Not applicable — it is applied to the skin, not swallowed.
precautions: For external use only and keep away from the eyes. Use for the full course as directed, and see your doctor if the infection does not improve or gets worse.

uses: Used to relieve pain and inflammation from conditions such as arthritis, muscle and joint injuries, back pain, period pain, and headaches, and to reduce fever.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset, heartburn, nausea, or dizziness. Seek help promptly for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or signs of an allergic reaction.
food: Take with food, milk, or a full glass of water to reduce stomach irritation.
precautions: Long-term or high use can raise the risk of stomach, kidney, and heart problems — use the lowest amount for the shortest time. Limit alcohol, and tell your doctor if you have ulcers, kidney or heart disease, or take blood thinners.

uses: Eye drops used to reduce pain and inflammation in the eye, most often after eye (such as cataract) surgery.
sideEffects: May cause temporary eye stinging or irritation, blurred vision just after use, or a feeling of something in the eye. Report worsening eye pain, redness, or vision changes.
food: Not applicable — this is an eye drop, not a medicine taken by mouth.
precautions: Wash hands before use and avoid touching the dropper tip to the eye to prevent contamination. If you wear contact lenses or use other eye drops, ask about timing and spacing between drops.

uses: Used to help people stop smoking by easing withdrawal symptoms and cravings, available as patches, gum, lozenges, sprays, or inhalers.
sideEffects: May cause headache, nausea, dizziness, hiccups, mouth or throat irritation (gum/lozenge), or skin irritation and vivid dreams (patch). Reduce use or seek advice if you feel a racing heart or strong nausea.
food: For gum and lozenges, avoid eating or drinking (especially acidic drinks like coffee or soda) just before and during use; patches are unrelated to meals.
precautions: Do not smoke while using it, and follow the plan to taper off over time. Tell your doctor if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, or are pregnant, and keep all forms away from children and pets.

uses: Used for short-term relief of acute pain and inflammation, such as musculoskeletal pain and period pain, in adults.
sideEffects: May cause stomach upset, nausea, or diarrhea. Because it can rarely cause liver injury, stop and seek help for yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, or upper-abdominal pain.
food: Take with or after food to reduce stomach irritation.
precautions: Use only short-term at the lowest effective amount, and avoid alcohol due to liver and stomach risks. Tell your doctor about any liver problems, and stop if signs of liver trouble appear; it is not recommended in children or pregnancy.

uses: Used to treat certain bacterial infections; oral forms may be used for some urinary, chest, or other infections, while eye and ear drop forms treat bacterial eye and ear infections. It does not work against viral illnesses.
sideEffects: Oral forms may cause nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, or headache; drops may cause brief stinging. Seek help for tendon pain or swelling, unusual nerve symptoms, or severe diarrhea.
food: Oral tablets can be taken with or without food, but separate them from dairy, antacids, and iron/zinc products, which reduce absorption.
precautions: Fluoroquinolones carry a risk of tendon, nerve, and heart-rhythm effects — stop and seek care for sudden tendon pain or tingling. Complete the full course, stay hydrated, and be cautious with sun exposure as skin may become more sensitive.

uses: Used to relieve allergy symptoms; the eye-drop form eases itchy, watery, allergic eyes, and the nasal spray form relieves allergic nasal symptoms such as sneezing and a runny nose.
sideEffects: May cause brief eye stinging or a bitter taste with drops, or nasal dryness, nosebleed, or mild drowsiness with the spray. Report persistent irritation or worsening symptoms.
food: Not applicable — it is applied to the eye or nose rather than swallowed.
precautions: Avoid touching the dropper or nozzle tip to the eye or nose to prevent contamination. If you wear contact lenses, ask about waiting before reinserting them after using the drops.

uses: Used to reduce stomach acid to treat heartburn and acid reflux (GERD), stomach and duodenal ulcers, and other conditions with too much acid; it also helps ulcers heal.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated; may cause headache, stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea, or gas. Long-term use may affect magnesium, vitamin B12, or bone health, so report muscle cramps or unusual symptoms.
food: Best taken before a meal, usually in the morning; swallow capsules whole and do not crush them.
precautions: Use for the shortest time needed, and see a doctor if heartburn lasts, you have trouble swallowing, or you notice black stools. Tell your doctor about other medicines, as it can interact with some drugs (for example certain blood thinners).

uses: Used to prevent and treat nausea and vomiting, such as that caused by certain medicines, treatments, or surgery.
sideEffects: Common effects include headache, constipation, and tiredness. Rarely it can affect the heart rhythm, so seek help for fainting, palpitations, or a very irregular heartbeat.
food: Can usually be taken with or without food.
precautions: Tell your doctor about any heart rhythm problems or other medicines you take, as some combinations can affect the heartbeat.

uses: Used to replace water and salts lost during diarrhoea, vomiting, or excessive sweating, helping to prevent or treat dehydration.
sideEffects: Generally very well tolerated; mild nausea or vomiting can occur, especially if the solution is drunk too quickly.
food: Can be taken regardless of meals; sip the prepared solution slowly throughout the day.
precautions: Mix only with the correct amount of clean, safe water and do not add extra sugar or salt. Seek medical help if there is severe dehydration, ongoing vomiting, blood in the stool, or symptoms in a very young child.

class: Antacid with a local numbing agent
uses: Used to relieve heartburn, acidity, and stomach or food-pipe discomfort by neutralising stomach acid and numbing the irritated lining.
sideEffects: May cause constipation or diarrhoea and a temporary numb feeling in the mouth. These are usually mild.
food: Often taken between meals or at bedtime; follow the label or your pharmacist's advice.
precautions: Antacids can reduce the absorption of other medicines, so take them a couple of hours apart. Use with caution if you have kidney problems.

uses: Used for short-term relief of a blocked or stuffy nose from colds, allergies, or sinus congestion.
sideEffects: May cause nasal stinging, dryness, or sneezing. Overuse can lead to worsening rebound congestion.
food: Not related to food, as it is used in the nose.
precautions: Do not use for more than a few days in a row to avoid rebound stuffiness. Use with caution if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or thyroid problems.

uses: Used to reduce stomach acid in conditions such as acid reflux, heartburn, and stomach or intestinal ulcers.
sideEffects: Common effects include headache, diarrhoea, and stomach upset. Long-term use may lower magnesium or vitamin B12 levels.
food: Usually taken before a meal, often in the morning.
precautions: Tell your doctor if you take it long term or notice ongoing symptoms. Let your pharmacist know your other medicines, as absorption of some drugs can change.

class: Acid-reducer (PPI) combined with a gut-movement/anti-nausea medicine
uses: Used for acid reflux and heartburn that also comes with bloating, nausea, or a feeling of fullness, by reducing acid and helping the stomach empty.
sideEffects: May cause headache, dry mouth, or stomach upset. Rarely the domperidone part can affect heart rhythm.
food: Usually taken before a meal.
precautions: Tell your doctor about any heart problems or other medicines you take. It is generally meant for short-term use unless advised otherwise.

uses: Used to relieve mild to moderate pain such as headache, body aches, and toothache, and to bring down fever.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated at recommended amounts. Taking too much can seriously damage the liver, so never exceed the label limit.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not exceed the recommended amount and avoid combining it with other products that also contain paracetamol. Be cautious with regular alcohol use or liver problems.

class: Cold & flu combination (pain/fever reliever + decongestant + antihistamine)
uses: Used for short-term relief of cold and flu symptoms such as fever, aches, blocked nose, sneezing, and runny nose.
sideEffects: May cause drowsiness, dry mouth, or a faster heartbeat. Seek help if you feel very unwell or notice a pounding heartbeat.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: It can cause drowsiness, so avoid driving and alcohol until you know how it affects you. Use with caution with high blood pressure or heart disease, and avoid other paracetamol-containing products.

uses: Used for short-term relief of a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, and other cold or allergy symptoms.
sideEffects: May cause drowsiness, dry mouth, and sometimes a faster heartbeat.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: It can cause drowsiness, so avoid driving and alcohol until you know how it affects you. Use with caution if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or an enlarged prostate.

uses: Used to treat constipation or to clear the bowel before certain medical procedures by drawing water into the stool.
sideEffects: May cause bloating, cramping, nausea, or loose stools. Drinking it too fast can worsen nausea.
food: Mixed with water and taken as directed; follow the label about timing around meals.
precautions: Drink plenty of fluids while using it. Do not use if you have a suspected bowel blockage, and check with a doctor if you have severe stomach pain or ongoing symptoms.

uses: Used to relieve dryness, irritation, and a gritty or burning feeling in the eyes.
sideEffects: May cause brief blurred vision or mild stinging right after use, which usually settles quickly.
