food: Not applicable, as these are eye drops.
precautions: Do not let the dropper tip touch your eye or any surface. If you wear soft contact lenses, follow the label about removing them before use.

uses: Used to clean and disinfect the skin, minor cuts and grazes, and as a gargle or mouthwash for some throat and mouth conditions.
sideEffects: May cause temporary skin staining, stinging, or irritation. Allergic skin reactions can occur in some people.
food: Not applicable, as it is used on the skin or as a mouth rinse rather than swallowed.
precautions: For external or rinse use only unless a doctor advises otherwise. Avoid on large or deep wounds and use with caution if you have thyroid problems or an iodine allergy.

uses: Used to reduce inflammation, redness, and swelling in the eye, such as after eye surgery or certain eye conditions.
sideEffects: May cause temporary blurred vision or stinging. Prolonged use can raise eye pressure or increase the risk of eye infection.
food: Not applicable, as these are eye drops; shake well before use if the label says so.
precautions: Use only for as long as prescribed and attend any eye check-ups. Do not stop a long course suddenly without advice, and do not let the dropper tip touch your eye.

uses: Used to treat certain types of nerve pain, some seizure disorders, and in some cases anxiety.
sideEffects: Common effects include dizziness, drowsiness, blurred vision, weight gain, and swelling of the hands or feet.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not stop it suddenly, as this should be done gradually under guidance. It can cause drowsiness and has a potential for dependence, so avoid alcohol and take exactly as prescribed.

uses: Used for allergy symptoms, nausea and vomiting, and sometimes to help with short-term sleep or before travel.
sideEffects: Commonly causes drowsiness, dry mouth, and blurred vision.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: It causes marked drowsiness, so avoid driving and alcohol until you know how it affects you. It is generally not suitable for young children, so follow age advice on the label.

uses: Used to help meet daily protein needs, for example to support muscle maintenance, recovery, or when dietary intake is inadequate.
sideEffects: May cause bloating, gas, or stomach discomfort, especially in people sensitive to milk sugar (lactose).
food: Can be mixed with water or milk and taken at various times of day; follow the product label.
precautions: Drink enough fluids and use with caution if you have kidney disease or are advised to limit protein. It is a supplement, not a replacement for a balanced diet or medical treatment.

uses: Used to reduce stomach acid in conditions such as acid reflux, heartburn, and stomach or intestinal ulcers.
sideEffects: Common effects include headache, diarrhoea, and stomach upset. Long-term use may lower magnesium or vitamin B12 levels.
food: Usually taken before a meal.
precautions: Tell your doctor if symptoms continue or you use it long term. Let your pharmacist know your other medicines, as absorption of some drugs can change.

uses: Used to lower high blood pressure, treat heart failure, and protect the heart and kidneys in certain conditions.
sideEffects: May cause a dry cough, dizziness, and tiredness. Rarely it can cause swelling of the face, lips, or throat, which needs urgent medical help.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Avoid during pregnancy and tell your doctor if you may become pregnant. Stand up slowly to reduce dizziness, and your doctor may check your kidney function and potassium levels.

uses: Used to prevent and treat blood clots, and to lower the risk of stroke in certain heart-rhythm and vascular conditions.
sideEffects: The main effect is easier bleeding or bruising. Seek urgent help for unusual or heavy bleeding, black stools, or coughing up blood.
food: Some strengths should be taken with food while others need not be; follow the label or your pharmacist's advice.
precautions: Do not stop taking it without medical advice, as this raises clot risk. Tell any doctor or dentist that you take it, and be cautious with other medicines, supplements, or alcohol that can increase bleeding.

uses: Used to lower high cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, alongside diet and lifestyle changes.
sideEffects: May cause muscle aches, headache, or stomach upset. Report severe or unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness promptly.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Avoid during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Limit alcohol, report significant muscle pain, and tell your doctor about other medicines as some can interact.

uses: A friendly yeast used to support gut health, often to help with diarrhea, including diarrhea linked to antibiotics or travel. It may help restore the natural balance of organisms in the gut.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated; some people notice mild gas, bloating, or constipation. Rarely, people with a weakened immune system or a central venous catheter can develop serious infections, so seek medical advice in those situations.
food: Can generally be taken with or without food; follow the label, and if you are also on antibiotics, space them apart as directed.
precautions: Not recommended for people who are seriously ill, have very weak immune systems, or have a central line. Avoid opening capsules near such patients, and check with a doctor if symptoms are severe or last more than a couple of days.

uses: Opens up the airways to relieve wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath in asthma and other lung conditions. It is typically used as a fast-acting reliever when symptoms flare.
sideEffects: May cause a fast or pounding heartbeat, shakiness (tremor), headache, or feeling jittery. Seek urgent help if your breathing does not improve or gets worse after using your reliever.
food: Not related to food, as it is usually breathed in through an inhaler or nebulizer; follow the label.
precautions: If you need your reliever more and more often, your condition may not be well controlled, so contact your doctor. Use the correct inhaler technique and tell your doctor about heart problems or an overactive thyroid.

class: Combination controller inhaler (long-acting bronchodilator + inhaled steroid)
uses: A daily preventer inhaler for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) that helps keep the airways open and reduces inflammation over time. It is used regularly to prevent symptoms, not for sudden attacks.
sideEffects: Common effects include hoarse voice, throat irritation, and oral thrush (a white mouth/throat infection). Rinsing your mouth after use helps; seek help for worsening breathing or signs of infection.
food: Not related to food, as it is inhaled; follow the label.
precautions: This is a preventer and does not relieve a sudden attack, so keep a quick-relief inhaler handy. Use it regularly as prescribed and do not stop suddenly; rinse your mouth after each dose to lower the risk of thrush.

uses: Used to treat depression and several anxiety-related conditions such as panic, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress. It works by helping balance a mood-related chemical (serotonin) in the brain.
sideEffects: May cause nausea, diarrhea, headache, trouble sleeping, or sexual side effects, which often ease over the first few weeks. Seek urgent help for new or worsening thoughts of self-harm, or for agitation, confusion, and a racing heart.
food: Can be taken with or without food; taking it with food may reduce stomach upset.
precautions: It can take a few weeks to work fully, and you should not stop it suddenly, as this can cause withdrawal effects. Tell your doctor about other medicines (especially other serotonin-raising drugs), avoid heavy alcohol use, and inform your doctor if pregnant or breastfeeding.

uses: Helps lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes by increasing the body's own insulin release after meals. It is usually used alongside diet, exercise, and sometimes other diabetes medicines.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; possible effects include headache, stuffy nose, or upper respiratory symptoms. Rarely it can cause severe abdominal pain (possible pancreas inflammation) or joint pain, so seek help if these occur.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: On its own it rarely causes low blood sugar, but this risk rises when combined with certain other diabetes drugs. Tell your doctor about kidney problems or any history of pancreas issues, and report severe stomach pain promptly.

uses: Relieves heartburn, acid reflux, and indigestion by neutralizing stomach acid and forming a protective 'raft' that floats on stomach contents to reduce acid coming back up. It is often used for symptom relief after meals.
sideEffects: Usually mild; may cause burping, bloating, or occasional constipation or loose stools. Seek advice if heartburn is frequent, severe, or does not improve.
food: Best taken after meals and at bedtime, when reflux tends to occur; follow the label.
precautions: Because it contains sodium and calcium, use caution if you are on a low-salt diet, have kidney problems, or take other calcium products. Antacids can affect the absorption of some other medicines, so separate them by a couple of hours.

uses: A fizzy remedy used to relieve indigestion and heartburn by neutralizing stomach acid, and in some products to make the urine less acidic to ease the discomfort of a mild urinary infection. Uses depend on the specific product.
sideEffects: May cause burping, bloating, or gas; too much can upset the body's acid balance. Seek advice if symptoms persist or you feel unwell.
food: Follow the label; antacid use is often after meals, while urinary products are usually taken with plenty of water.
precautions: It contains sodium, so use caution if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney problems, or are on a low-salt diet. It can interact with several medicines and is not for long-term regular use without medical advice.

uses: Used in many forms to provide salt and water, such as saline nasal sprays and rinses for congestion, eye or wound irrigation, and fluids given in hospital. The purpose depends on the specific product.
sideEffects: Generally very safe when used as directed; nasal or eye forms may cause brief stinging or dripping. Fluids given by drip can occasionally cause swelling or salt imbalances, which are monitored by staff.
food: Not related to food for sprays, rinses, or drips; follow the product label.
precautions: Use the strength intended for your purpose, as concentrated salt solutions are not for the same uses as ordinary saline. If you have heart, kidney, or blood-pressure problems, check with a doctor before using salt-containing products regularly.

class: Water tablet / blood-pressure medicine (potassium-sparing diuretic, aldosterone blocker)
uses: Helps the body remove excess fluid and lower blood pressure while holding on to potassium, and is used in heart failure, fluid buildup, and certain hormone-related conditions. It is also sometimes used for hormonal acne and excess hair growth.
sideEffects: Can raise potassium levels, cause dizziness or tiredness, and in some people breast tenderness or enlargement and menstrual changes. Seek help for muscle weakness, an irregular heartbeat, or severe dizziness.
food: Best taken with food to reduce stomach upset and improve absorption.
precautions: Avoid extra potassium (supplements or salt substitutes) unless told otherwise, as high potassium can be dangerous. Your doctor will monitor blood tests, and you should mention kidney problems or other blood-pressure medicines you take.

uses: Forms a protective coating over ulcers and irritated areas in the stomach and upper gut, helping them heal and shielding them from acid. It is used for stomach and duodenal ulcers and related irritation.
sideEffects: The most common effect is constipation; some people get dry mouth, nausea, or indigestion. Side effects are usually mild.
food: Usually taken on an empty stomach, typically before meals and at bedtime; follow the label.
precautions: It can reduce absorption of many other medicines, so take other drugs a couple of hours apart. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as it contains aluminum, and use caution with long-term use.

uses: Lowers blood pressure by relaxing and widening blood vessels, and helps protect the heart and kidneys in some patients. It is used for high blood pressure and to reduce cardiovascular risk.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated; may cause dizziness (especially when standing), back or sinus symptoms, and occasionally raised potassium. Seek help for fainting, swelling of the face or throat, or a very low heart rate.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not use in pregnancy, as it can harm the baby; tell your doctor if you may become pregnant. Rise slowly to avoid dizziness, stay hydrated, and use caution with potassium supplements or salt substitutes and with kidney problems.

class: Combination blood-pressure medicine (ARB + calcium channel blocker)
uses: Combines two blood-pressure medicines in one tablet to relax blood vessels and lower blood pressure more effectively than either alone. It is used when a single medicine is not enough to control blood pressure.
sideEffects: May cause dizziness, ankle or leg swelling, flushing, or headache. Seek help for fainting, significant swelling, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: Do not use in pregnancy because the ARB part can harm the baby. Rise slowly to avoid dizziness, and tell your doctor about kidney or liver problems, grapefruit intake, and other blood-pressure or potassium-affecting medicines.

uses: Treats fungal infections of the skin, nails, and feet (such as ringworm, athlete's foot, and fungal nail infections). It comes as tablets for more stubborn infections and as creams for skin infections.
sideEffects: Tablets may cause stomach upset, headache, rash, or a temporary change in taste or smell; creams may cause local irritation. Seek prompt help for signs of liver problems (yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness) or a serious rash.
food: Tablets can be taken with or without food; apply creams to clean, dry skin as directed.
precautions: Nail and skin infections can take weeks to months to clear, so complete the full course. With tablets, tell your doctor about liver problems and other medicines, as liver monitoring may be needed.

uses: Most often used as eye drops to lower pressure inside the eye in glaucoma or ocular hypertension; in tablet form it can treat high blood pressure and other heart-related conditions. The eye drops help protect vision by reducing eye pressure.
sideEffects: Eye drops may cause brief stinging, blurred vision, or dry eyes, and can occasionally slow the heart or affect breathing. Seek help for wheezing, a very slow heartbeat, or fainting.
food: Not applicable to eye drops; if taken as tablets, follow the label regarding food.
precautions: Even eye drops can be absorbed into the body, so caution is needed with asthma, breathing problems, or a slow heart rate. Press gently on the inner corner of the eye after dosing to limit absorption, and do not stop suddenly without medical advice.

uses: A once-daily maintenance inhaler that keeps the airways open in COPD and, in some cases, asthma. It is used regularly to prevent breathlessness, not to relieve a sudden attack.
sideEffects: Commonly causes dry mouth; some people get constipation, a sore throat, or urinary difficulty. Seek help for eye pain or sudden vision changes, or if breathing suddenly worsens.
food: Not related to food, as it is inhaled; follow the label.
precautions: This is a preventer, so keep a quick-relief inhaler for sudden symptoms. Avoid getting the powder in your eyes, and tell your doctor about glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or bladder problems.

uses: An antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections; as eye drops or ointment for eye infections, as an inhaled form for certain chronic lung infections, and by injection in hospitals for serious infections. It works by killing the bacteria causing the infection.
sideEffects: Eye forms may cause brief stinging, redness, or blurred vision; inhaled forms may cause cough or voice changes. Injected forms can affect hearing, balance, and the kidneys, so these are closely monitored.
food: Not related to food for eye or inhaled forms; injectable use is managed by healthcare staff.
precautions: Use only for the infection it was prescribed for and finish the course as directed. Report any change in hearing, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or reduced urination, especially with injected or inhaled forms.

uses: An eye drop or ointment that combines an antibiotic to fight bacterial infection with a steroid to reduce inflammation and swelling in the eye. It is used for certain eye infections or inflammation and after some eye surgery.
sideEffects: May cause brief stinging, blurred vision, or eye irritation. Long or repeated use can raise eye pressure or delay healing, so seek advice for eye pain, worsening vision, or symptoms that do not improve.
food: Not applicable, as it is used in the eye; follow the label.
precautions: Because it contains a steroid, do not use longer than prescribed, as this can raise eye pressure or mask a worsening infection. Do not touch the dropper tip to the eye, and remove contact lenses before use unless told otherwise.

uses: Helps control blood sugar in type 2 diabetes by boosting the body's own insulin response to meals and reducing excess sugar release. It is usually combined with diet, exercise, and sometimes other diabetes medicines.
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; possible effects include dizziness, headache, or tremor. Rarely it can affect the liver or cause severe abdominal pain (possible pancreas inflammation), so seek help for yellowing skin/eyes or severe stomach pain.
food: Can be taken with or without food.
precautions: On its own it rarely causes low blood sugar, but the risk rises when combined with certain other diabetes drugs. Your doctor may check liver blood tests, and you should report severe stomach pain or signs of liver trouble.

uses: Provides a group of B vitamins together with vitamin C to help fill dietary gaps and support normal energy, nerve function, and general health. It is often used to prevent or correct mild vitamin shortfalls.
sideEffects: Usually well tolerated; may cause mild stomach upset, and can turn the urine bright yellow, which is harmless. Very high intakes over time can cause other effects, so stick to recommended amounts.
food: Best taken with food to reduce stomach upset.
precautions: It is a supplement, not a substitute for a balanced diet or treatment of a diagnosed deficiency. Tell your doctor if you take other supplements or have kidney stones, and avoid doubling up on products containing the same vitamins.

uses: Relieves a blocked or stuffy nose from colds, allergies, or sinus congestion by shrinking swollen blood vessels in the nose. It provides fast, temporary relief of nasal congestion.
sideEffects: May cause brief stinging, dryness, or sneezing in the nose. Overuse can lead to rebound congestion (a worse blocked nose when you stop), and occasionally headache or a racing heart.
food: Not related to food, as it is used in the nose; follow the label.
precautions: Do not use for more than a few days in a row to avoid rebound congestion. Use with caution if you have high blood pressure, heart problems, or thyroid issues, and do not share the spray to avoid spreading infection.
